::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[solve equilibrium points and the equation from given derivatives](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/1928927/solve-equilibrium-points-and-the-equation-from-given-derivatives), asked by [user365442](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/365442/user365442) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2016-09-16; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> The question shows this:
> >$$\frac{dN}{dt} = \frac{1}{4} N(t) \left( 1 - \frac{N(t)}{225}\right) - \frac{7}{2}$$
>
> How can we solve the equation as we don't know what is the power of t present in the function N?
:::

With a little bit of arithmetic we can rewrite the equation as
$$\frac{dN}{dt} = -\frac{N^2 - 225N + 3150}{900}$$
Where $N$ is just shorthand for $N(t)$.

The question title asks about *equilibrium points*.  Those are the constant solutions to this differential equation.  If $N(t)$ is constant, $\frac{dN}{dt} = 0$.  This is equivalent to
$$N^2 - 225N+3150 = 0 \implies (N-15)(N-210) = 0$$
So there are two equilibria: $N(t) \equiv 15$ and $N(t) \equiv 210$.

In the question you wondered how to solve for $N(t)$ “when we don't know the power of $t$ present in $N$.”  Differential equations are, in general, hard to solve.  There's no guarantee that $N(t)$ is a power function to begin with.  But notice that we found the equilibria without finding $N(t)$ explicitly.  In DE you can say a lot *about* the solutions without knowing their closed-form expression.

As it turns out, this DE is what we call *separable* and can be solved explicitly.  We write
$$\frac{dN}{(N-15)(N-210)} = - \frac{1}{900} \,dt
    \implies
    \int\frac{dN}{(N-15)(N-210)} = - \int\frac{1}{900} \,dt$$
At first blush, this looks like voodoo math but it is grounded in rigor.  In any case, the right-hand side is easily integrated but the left-hand side requires partial fractions:
$$\frac{1}{(N-15)(N-210)} = \frac{1}{195}\left(\frac{1}{N-210} - \frac{1}{N-15}\right)$$
Moving the constant to the other side, we now have
$$\int\left(\frac{1}{N-210} - \frac{1}{N-15}\right)\,dN
= -\int\frac{195}{900}\,dt = - \int \frac{13}{60} \,dt$$
Now we can integrate!
$$\ln\left|\frac{N-210}{N-15}\right| = -\frac{13t}{60} + C$$
where $C$ is some constant depending on the initial conditions of $N(t)$.
Exponentiating,
$$\frac{N-210}{N-15} = e^{-13t/60 + C} = e^C e^{-13t/60} = C_1   e^{-13t/60}$$
This can be solved for $N$ in terms of $t$:
$$\begin{align*}
    N-210 &= C_1 e^{-13t/60}(N-15)\\\implies
    e^{13t/60}N - 210 e^{13t/60} &= C_1 N - 15 C_1 \\\implies
    N\left(e^{13t/60}-C_1\right) &= 210 e^{13t/60}- 15 C_1 \\\implies
    N(t) &= \frac{210 e^{13t/60}- 15 C_1}{e^{13t/60}-C_1}
\end{align*}$$
(acknowledgements to [Wolfram Alpha](http://bit.ly/2cOeHG3))

Now that we have the explicit form for $N(t)$, notice that
$$\begin{align*}
    \lim_{t\to+\infty} N(t) &= 210 \\
    \lim_{t\to-\infty} N(t) &= 15
\end{align*}$$
and these are our two equilibrium solutions.  This means 210 is a stable equilibrium and 15 is unstable.  But again, most of the question can be answered *without* solving the equation explicitly.
